data.title: Eval harness: planted-fault fixture kind (data), scoring, miss-rate and enable-by-default verdict
Eval harness: standard fake kit (clock, agent, meters, control plane, hub, bench, vendor tool)
Eval harness: runner, miss-rate report surface and enable-by-default gate

data.body:
Twelve evaluation tasks and fifty acceptance tasks each build their own fixtures; one harness gives a fixture registry, a standard fake kit, a miss-rate report per workflow and the rule that a workflow is enabled by default only after it catches its planted set; extends the live-recorded fixtures (B-ac-fixtures).

CONFORMANCE (D-universal-principles, rules r-everything-configurable, r-everything-managed, r-reuse-core): every number is a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt; every definition this task adds (kind, template, gate, lens, role, lint set, importer, pack, job) is a record kind under the record contract RC1-RC12 (add, edit, remove as a tombstone, review and history, search, recall and RAG export, logged events and replay restore); every shipped default is overridable per project and per org; search for an existing function and extend the shared engines (P-shared-engines) instead of writing a second one; files under 20 KB.

Split into: SE-eval-harness.1, SE-eval-harness.2, SE-eval-harness.3.

data.claim: A TOML evalfixture kind rides the generic record surface, and scoring by word match gives a deterministic miss rate
data.falsifier: the kind failing the shared add/show/edit/remove/search test, or the scorer giving different results on a rerun
data.mechanism: kinddata loads templates/kinds/*.toml; planted entries id=word|word are matched case-insensitively against finding text
data.probe_output: evalfixture passes the packaged-kind add/show/edit/remove cycle; scorer tests 6 passed
data.question: Can planted-fault fixtures be a TOML data kind with a pure word-match scorer, no second engine?

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard is documented and reported as counting *planted-fault* fixtures ("needs at least {min_fixtures} planted-fault fixture(s); has {row['fixtures']}"), but `report` fills `fixtures` with `len(rows)`, i.e. every `Score` recorded for the workflow — including clean fixtures that plant nothing. A fixture with `planted = []` yields a `Score` with `planted == 0`, `missed == 0`, and enters `by` just like any other, so it inflates the count that this check consumes.

Concrete failure: with `min_fixtures = 3`, a workflow evaluated on three fixtures where two have no `planted` entries and the third has a single planted fault that is caught produces `row["fixtures"] == 3 >= 3`, `miss_rate == 0.0`, and `enable_by_default` returns `(True, ...)` — the workflow is enabled by default although only one planted-fault fixture was ever exercised, which is exactly the evidence the reason string claims was required. A harness that adds clean fixtures (the kind this module explicitly models, see the "on a clean fixture, a false positive" note) can therefore push a thinly-tested workflow past the `min_fixtures` gate; the check should count fixtures with `s.planted > 0` (or the parameter should be compared against `sum(1 for s in rows if s.planted)`).

chunk_findings.detail: The `min_fixtures` gate compares `row["fixtures"]`, which `report` computes as `len(rows)` — the count of *all* fixtures a workflow was scored on — but the failure message and the intent say the gate is over *planted-fault* fixtures ("needs at least {min_fixtures} planted-fault fixture(s)"). Because the module's own docstring explicitly contemplates clean fixtures ("on a clean fixture, a false positive"), a clean fixture inflates the count. Concrete input: `min_fixtures=2`, `max_miss_rate=0.0`, workflow `W` with one planted-fault fixture whose single fault is caught (`Score(fixture="a", workflow="W", caught=("f1",), missed=(), extra=())`) plus one clean fixture producing only an unmatched finding (`Score(fixture="b", workflow="W", caught=(), missed=(), extra=("noise",))`). Then `fixtures=2`, `planted=1`, `miss_rate=0.0`, and the first branch `row["fixtures"] < min_fixtures` is False, so `enable_by_default` returns `(True, "caught its planted set (1 faults in 2 fixtures)")`. The workflow is enabled by default after catching exactly one planted fault, although `min_fixtures=2` was supposed to require two planted-fault fixtures — i.e. the gate is weaker than the requirement it reports, so coverage requirements silently degrade as clean fixtures are added.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/evalharness.py:111 (enable_by_default / report row["fixtures"])

chunk_findings.detail: `planted` is the fixture's answer key — the fault ids and the exact words a finding must contain to be scored as caught (`planted = ["sql=injection|concat", "race=lock"]` in the harness test). This change puts that key into the record's `text` set, i.e. it is indexed/searched/displayed like any other searchable field, in the same record kind that lives in the ordinary record store the evaluated workflow runs against. The harness's own `render = "{id} [{workflow}] {title}"` deliberately keeps `planted` out of the rendered form, so the record is meant to present only the input to the workflow under test; `text` contradicts that by exposing the ground truth alongside it. Concretely: for a fixture whose key is `sql=injection|concat`, any reader/search over the store sees `sql`, `injection`, `concat` (and no test constrains the `text` set, so this passes CI), letting a workflow emit findings containing those words, be scored `caught` on every fault, report `miss_rate == 0` and be enabled by default although it located nothing — exactly the outcome a planted-fault fixture exists to prevent. Only the material to review (`input`, plus descriptive fields such as `tags`) belongs in `text`; `planted` must not be reachable by the workflow being scored.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/kinds/evalfixture.toml:3 (`text = ["input", "planted", "tags"]`)

data.reason: 2 finding(s)

chunk_findings.detail: `enable_by_default` advertises `row: Mapping[str, Any] | None` and explicitly guards the missing-row case with `have = row["planted_fixtures"] if row else 0`, but the `None` path is only safe when `min_fixtures >= 1`. With `row=None` and `min_fixtures=0` (a legitimate setting for a config knob that means "no fixture minimum"), the first guard `if have < min_fixtures` is `0 < 0` → False, so execution falls through to `rate = row["miss_rate"]` and raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` instead of returning the documented `(False, reason)` verdict. The fixture-count guard should return early for `row is None` (or short-circuit before indexing), otherwise a caller that passes `None` for a workflow with no measurements gets a crash rather than "no fault is planted in its fixtures, so nothing was measured".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/evalharness.py:enable_by_default

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard is documented and reported as counting *planted-fault* fixtures ("needs at least {min_fixtures} planted-fault fixture(s); has {row['fixtures']}"), but `report` fills `fixtures` with `len(rows)`, i.e. every `Score` recorded for the workflow — including clean fixtures that plant nothing. A fixture with `planted = []` yields a `Score` with `planted == 0`, `missed == 0`, and enters `by` just like any other, so it inflates the count that this check consumes.

Concrete failure: with `min_fixtures = 3`, a workflow evaluated on three fixtures where two have no `planted` entries and the third has a single planted fault that is caught produces `row["fixtures"] == 3 >= 3`, `miss_rate == 0.0`, and `enable_by_default` returns `(True, ...)` — the workflow is enabled by default although only one planted-fault fixture was ever exercised, which is exactly the evidence the reason string claims was required. A harness that adds clean fixtures (the kind this module explicitly models, see the "on a clean fixture, a false positive" note) can therefore push a thinly-tested workflow past the `min_fixtures` gate; the check should count fixtures with `s.planted > 0` (or the parameter should be compared against `sum(1 for s in rows if s.planted)`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/evalharness.py:enable_by_default (the `row["fixtures"] < min_fixtures` check)

chunk_findings.detail: The old guard was `if not row or row["fixtures"] < min_fixtures:`, which returned `False` for a missing/empty row unconditionally. The new code computes `have = row["planted_fixtures"] if row else 0` and only returns early when `have < min_fixtures`. When `min_fixtures <= 0` (a caller that configures no minimum) and `row` is `None` or `{}`, `have` becomes `0`, `0 < 0` is false, and control falls through to `rate = row["miss_rate"]`, which raises `TypeError` on `None` (or `KeyError` on `{}`) instead of returning `(False, ...)` as before. Concrete call: `enable_by_default(None, 0)` previously returned a `(False, "needs at least 0 planted-fault fixture(s); has 0")`; now it crashes. Restoring an explicit `not row` short-circuit (or `row or {}` default) would keep the missing-row case total.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/evalharness.py:enable_by_default (row=None/empty path)

chunk_findings.detail:
`FakeAgent.__call__` declares `prompt` as an ordinary named parameter, so a caller may legitimately invoke the fake as `agent(prompt="do X")`. In that case `_Scripted._next` records the call as `((), {"prompt": "do X"})`, and the `prompts` property does `c[0][0]` on an empty positional-tuple, raising `IndexError: tuple index out of range` instead of returning `["do X"]`. Concrete demo:

    a = FakeAgent(["ok"])
    a(prompt="do X")      # returns "ok"
    a.prompts             # <- IndexError, not ["do X"]

The call succeeds, so the failure surfaces only later when a test inspects what was prompted (which is the primary reason this fake exists), and it fails with an opaque indexing error rather than the missing-prompt signal. `prompts` should read the prompt from `kw` when no positional argument was given (e.g. `c[0][0] if c[0] else c[1]["prompt"]`).

chunk_findings.detail:
`FakeAgent.__call__` declares `prompt` as an ordinary named parameter, so a caller may legitimately invoke the fake as `agent(prompt="do X")`. In that case `_Scripted._next` records the call as `((), {"prompt": "do X"})`, and the `prompts` property does `c[0][0]` on an empty positional-tuple, raising `IndexError: tuple index out of range` instead of returning `["do X"]`. Concrete demo:

    a = FakeAgent(["ok"])
    a(prompt="do X")      # returns "ok"
    a.prompts             # <- IndexError, not ["do X"]

The call succeeds, so the failure surfaces only later when a test inspects what was prompted (which is the primary reason this fake exists), and it fails with an opaque indexing error rather than the missing-prompt signal. `prompts` should read the prompt from `kw` when no positional argument was given (e.g. `c[0][0] if c[0] else c[1]["prompt"]`).

chunk_findings.detail:
`fixtures()` declares `workflow: str = ""` with the docstring "those of `workflow` when given", i.e. the empty default is meant to mean "all fixtures". But the default is never special-cased: the function unconditionally builds `filters={"workflow": workflow}` and hands it to `R.record_list`. `record_list` takes a `filters` mapping, which is an exact-match filter; an empty string is a legitimate (truthy-dict) filter value, so `fixtures(repo)` asks for records whose `workflow` field equals `""`. Since every `evalfixture` record carries a real workflow name, that query returns zero rows, so `rows == []`, `out == []`.

The public entry point hits exactly this path: `report(repo, workflows)` calls `run(fixtures(repo), workflows)` with no workflow argument, so `EH.report` is fed an empty score list. The consequence is that the enable-by-default gate always sees zero fixtures for every registered workflow and can never report a verdict — the feature is inert, and, depending on how `EH.report` treats an absent workflow, may also vacuously pass `min_fixtures`. The fix is to only add the `workflow` key when it is non-empty (or pass `None` and have `record_list` skip it), matching the documented "when given" semantics.

chunk_findings.detail: `fixtures(repo, workflow="")` always passes `filters={"workflow": workflow}`, even when `workflow` is the empty default, while its own docstring promises "those of `workflow` when given" — i.e. all fixtures when not given. `report()` is the primary entry point of the enable-by-default gate and calls `fixtures(repo)` with no workflow, so it takes exactly this path. For any `record_list` that applies `filters` as equality (the natural reading of a `filters` mapping), `workflow == ""` matches no `evalfixture` record (the fixtures carry a real workflow name such as the gate/`evalkit` fake), so `rows` is empty, `run(...)` scores nothing, and `EH.report(...)` returns an empty report for every workflow — the miss-rate/`min_fixtures` verdicts are never produced and the gate can never enable by default. The filter should be applied only when `workflow` is non-empty (e.g. omit `filters` for the default), or `report()` should pass the workflow set it actually wants scored. Please confirm `record_list` does not silently drop falsy filter values; if it does, this path is fine and only the conditional-filter intent is muddied.

chunk_findings.detail:
The module declares the unlabelled level as a fixed code constant and its comment says "a project may relabel it, so it is named here once", but nothing makes it data or checks that it exists in the vocabulary, and `parse` rejects any top-level key other than `level`/`scan`, so a project *cannot* designate a different unlabelled level. `scan_level` then uses it as a bound default parameter:

    def scan_level(self, found, floor: str = UNLABELLED) -> str:
        ...
        return self.highest([floor, *hits])   # rank(floor) -> self.levels["internal"].rank

`Vocabulary.__init__` validates scan values against the registered levels but never validates `UNLABELLED` itself, so any vocabulary that does not contain a level literally named `internal` loads fine and then fails at run time with a bare `KeyError: 'internal'` the first time `scan_level` is called without an explicit `floor` — e.g. `Vocabulary([Level("public", 0, True), Level("confidential", 1, False)], {"secret": "confidential"}).scan_level({"secret": 1})`, or the same situation after the packaged `templates/sensitivity.toml` (pure data, meant to be editable) is changed to name its lowest level anything else. Every other inconsistency in this file raises `SensitivityError` at parse time; this one is silent until first use, and the stated relabelling capability does not exist.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/core/sensitivity.py:24` (`UNLABELLED` / `Vocabulary.scan_level`)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `v.scan_level({"secret": 0, "unmapped": 4}, floor="public") == "public"` pins down that any detected kind that is absent from the `[scan]` mapping is silently dropped, and the result then falls to the floor. Combined with `may_send("public") is True` (asserted two tests earlier) this is fail-open: given redactor counts containing 4 hits of a kind the vocabulary has never heard of — a new pattern kind, a project-local pattern, or simply a renamed/typo'd kind in the config — `scan_level` reports `public` and the content is eligible to be sent to a model, which is precisely the outcome the registry exists to prevent. Contrast the sibling API `may_send`, which raises `KeyError` on an unknown level; here the same class of config drift is silently absorbed instead of being refused (the parametrised test refuses a `[scan]` entry pointing at a nonexistent level, but never a *counted* kind missing from `[scan]`). A conservative implementation (raise, or treat an unmapped kind as the highest level) is exactly what this test would forbid, so the defect is encoded in the assertion, not merely uncovered by it. The companion `test_every_scan_kind_is_one_the_redactor_counts` does not rescue this: it only checks the kinds produced by one fixed sample string, so it cannot establish that unmapped counts are unreachable.
